html:
The Kazakh famine of 1919 to 1922 was a mass starvation on the Kazakh steppe and in Turkestan during the Russian Civil War. Between about 400,000 and 750,000 people died, most of them Kazakhs.

Many causes came together. Herds had already been lost in the revolt of 1916 and its repression. Both Red and White armies seized livestock and grain. The Bolsheviks' forced grain collection, part of War Communism, stripped villages of food, while settlers who came under the Stolypin resettlement held much of the best land. Drought then ruined the harvests.

The famine was part of the wider Russian famine of 1921 and 1922, which killed millions. Foreign relief, mostly American, reached some areas. A second and far worse disaster followed ten years later, the Kazakh famine of 1930 to 1933.
